title: Of Foresight and Looking to the Ends of Affairs

keywords: of looking to the ends of affairs
full_text:
On the second day, the Second Wazir argued before King Azadbakht on the necessity of calculating the distant consequences of every deed: 'Sire, he who looks only at the immediate profit before his feet is like a child who reaches for a ripe fig, unmindful that a viper sleeps upon the branch.'

Bakhtiyar smiled in agreement, elaborating upon the principle of foresight:

'Your minister speaks a pearl of wisdom, O King! True intelligence is not measured by the cleverness with which one acts in the moment, but by the clarity with which one anticipates the end of affairs.

A deed begun in passionate haste without calculating its conclusion is like an arrow shot into the fog: it may strike an innocent friend or shatter upon stone.

The wise statesman plants seeds today whose fruit he may never eat, and avoids taking a path whose exit he has not examined. He weighs every decree upon the balance of time: "What will this word bring tomorrow? What will it bring in seven years? And how will history record it when our bones are dust?"

He who cultivates foresight builds stone aqueducts that endure for centuries, while the impulsive ruler builds houses of straw that collapse with the first autumn wind, as the chronicle of the Merchant and His Sons illustrates for all who have ears to hear.'
moral: Prudent foresight that considers the long-term consequences of actions protects a household from sudden ruin.
